nameStory: The distant scallop gets its name from being far from home in New England waters. Native to the western Central Pacific, this scallop has traveled thousands of miles from its usual tropical haunts to occasionally appear along our coast. When you find one here, it truly is a 'distant' visitor from across the world's oceans.
description: The distant scallop is a medium-sized bivalve mollusk with the classic fan-shaped shell that makes scallops instantly recognizable. Like all scallops, it has two hinged shells (called valves) that protect its soft body inside, with distinctive radiating ridges spreading out from the hinge like the ribs of a fan. This tropical species is edible and prized in its native Pacific waters. In New England, it's an extremely rare find that likely arrived as a hitchhiker on ships or in ballast water.

idTips.label: Fan-shaped shell
idTips.description: Classic scallop shape with two rounded, fan-like valves that feel smooth to slightly rough depending on wear, with a straight hinge line where they connect

idTips.label: Radiating ridges
idTips.description: Prominent ribs that fan out from the hinge to the shell edge, creating a textured surface you can feel with your fingers when running them from center to rim

idTips.label: Tropical appearance
idTips.description: Often more colorful or differently patterned than typical New England scallops, with shells that may show warmer tones or unusual markings

idTips.label: Size and weight
idTips.description: Medium-sized for a scallop, feeling substantial but not overly heavy in your palm, with shells that close tightly when fresh

habitat: In New England, distant scallops are found exclusively in marine environments, typically washed up on beaches or occasionally in shallow coastal waters. They prefer sandy or muddy bottoms in their native range, so any New England specimens would likely be found near similar substrates along our coast. Given their rarity here, they're most often discovered as single shells on beaches rather than living populations.

seasonality.spring: Beach-washed shells may appear after winter storms have stirred up unusual debris, making this the most likely time to spot specimens.
seasonality.summer: Warm water periods might occasionally bring live individuals north, though this remains extremely rare in New England waters.
seasonality.fall: Storm season can wash unusual shells ashore, including potential distant scallop specimens mixed with more common species.
seasonality.winter: Harsh weather and strong currents make this the least likely time to encounter this tropical species in our waters.

funFact: This scallop has somehow managed to cross the entire Pacific Ocean to occasionally show up in New England, making it one of the most well-traveled mollusks you could possibly find on our beaches – a true globetrotter of the shellfish world!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with bay scallops or sea scallops, our common local species. Look for unusual coloration, different ridge patterns, or shell proportions that seem 'off' compared to typical New England scallops. If a scallop shell looks tropical or exotic compared to the usual gray-brown locals, it might be this distant visitor.
contextualKnowledge: The distant scallop's presence in New England highlights how global shipping and changing ocean conditions can bring species far from their native ranges. Finding one here doesn't mean they're establishing populations – they're more likely individual travelers that won't survive our colder waters long-term.
compareHints: Since there are no other Bractechlamys species in New England, compare this with our native bay and sea scallops. The distant scallop often shows different coloration patterns and may have subtly different shell proportions or ridge spacing compared to our local species. Its tropical origin usually gives it a more exotic appearance than the typically muted tones of cold-water New England scallops.
